Failure of sensory and motor nerve-root signaling can contribute to clinical root dysfunction. The complete route from experimental conduction changes to human sacral and lower-limb deficits remains incompletely resolved.
Compression of the sacral parasympathetic autonomic fibers disrupts detrusor function, causing urinary retention with overflow incontinence.
Involvement of the sacral sensory roots produces perineal and perianal ("saddle") sensory loss.
Involvement of the sacral autonomic and somatic fibers to the anal sphincter disrupts continence, producing bowel incontinence and reduced anal tone.
Injury to the sacral autonomic and sensory roots impairs genital sensation and the autonomic control of arousal, producing sexual dysfunction.

nodes.description: Surgical decompression is the main treatment for MRI-confirmed compressive CES. WFNS consensus recommends surgery within 48 hours, preferably within 24 hours. Historical pooled studies associate earlier surgery with better outcomes, but a prospective UK cohort found no adjusted association between symptom-to-surgery time and bladder or disability outcomes. Most patients in that cohort underwent prompt surgery after referral, so it cannot establish that delaying treatment is safe. Retention at presentation does not preclude postoperative improvement.
